Ashaeiynn: Purnima Mahayagya — Sankalp Types, Akhand Deepak, Bhog/Samagri Offerings, and the Meaning of Havan

Part A — Akhand Deepak

1. What akhand deepak is for , per this teaching: An unbroken (continuously burning) lamp maintained at Ashaeiynn on behalf of devotees who cannot maintain their own lamp or daily japa at home, whether due to space, family circumstances, or other constraints.

2. Two types described: One dedicated to the guru (Baba), and one dedicated to one's kul devta (family/ancestral deity) — the mentor recommends the kul devta akhand deepak specifically , noting that kul devta blessing is described in this teaching as important for practical life matters (e.g., financial stagnation or plans repeatedly falling through), and that it is not necessary to know exactly who one's kul devta is in order to sponsor this lamp, since responsibility for directing the lamp's benefit is described as resting with the guru lineage, not the devotee.
Part B — Mahayagya Sankalp Types

1. Raksha-suraksha (pr otection) sankalp: Described as providing roughly 20-25 days of protective "shielding" from tantric attack, repeated negative influence, or pitru (ancestral)-related disturbance; can be taken for oneself, family members, or friends, including people not themselves connected to Ashaeiynn.

2. Jagriti (awakening) sankalp: Described as advancing a practitioner's bhakti (devotional) tattva, said to raise a practitioner "50 to 500 dimensions" (of fered as this teaching's own devotional metric, not a verifiable measurement) — framed as supporting faster spiritual growth rather than protection specifically .

3. Other sankalp types available at the Mahayagya: Standard negativity , pitru, and kul devta sankalps (normally taken at regular havan) can also be taken specifically during the Mahayagya; the stated advantage is that a much lar ger number of saints are said to be present during a Mahayagya than during a routine havan, increasing the chance, per this teaching, of a particular saint's blessing reaching the devotee.
Part C — Bhog and Samagri Offerings

1. The "parat" (offering tray) system: Two standard sizes are of fered — a smaller 5 kg tray (stated cost: 3,100 rupees, including three coconuts) and a lar ger 10 kg tray (stated cost: 4,100 rupees, including ten coconuts). These figures are recorded exactly as stated in the source recording for documentary purposes and should not be treated as current, live pricing — see the Bot Response Guidelines.

2. What the offering materials include, per the facility tour shown in this session: Eleven categories of items used in preparing the guru's bhog are described, including bajra (pearl millet), jau (barley), rice, general havan samagri, kand (a root item), dry fruits (almonds, raisins), lotus seeds (kamal gatta), lar ge cardamom, cashews, dried dates (chhuara), ghee, and coconut (sold separately in roughly 10 kg boxes).

3. Partial/single-item offerings: Devotees who do not wish to sponsor a full parat may instead of fer any single item from the above list (for example, only dry fruits, only rice, only ghee, or only a box of coconuts) in whatever quantity they choose, dedicated either to the guru or to their kul devta.

4. Milk and sweets offerings: Offered as a separate option from the food-grain/dry-fruit bhog described above; devotees wishing to of fer milk or sweets (laddoo, rasgulla, gulab jamun) may do so through the same payment-and-confirmation process.

5. Process for confirming an offering: Devotees are asked to make payment to Ashaeiynn's of ficial account and then send a payment screenshot to their assigned mentor , noting in writing what the of fering is for (e.g., milk, a specific bhog item, or the reason for the sankalp) so the of fering can be properly arranged on their behalf.
Part D — A Practitioner's Account of the Ongoing Akhand Ram Yajna

1. Context: The mentor conducting this session interviews a long-time havan practitioner (referred to as "V ijit bhai" in the source recording) who was, at the time of filming, roughly six to seven hours into that day's session of Ashaeiynn's ongoing, unbroken (akhand) Ram Yajna (fire ritual).

2. A personal account of physical difficulty over come, offer ed by the practitioner: He describes having a leg/knee injury that normally prevents him from sitting for extended periods, but states that he is able to sit for six to seven hours specifically during this havan, which he attributes, in his own account, to the guru's grace — recorded here as his personal testimony , not independently verified.

3. The practitioner's description of havan's significance, per this teaching: Havan is described as a "gateway" connecting to the wider cosmos, with fire (agni) serving as the medium that transforms physical of ferings into an ener gy form said to be transferred to dif ferent lokas (realms) and dimensions; he encourages listeners to experience this for themselves rather than rely solely on secondhand description.
4. How long this specific yajna has been running: Described as continuously ongoing for approximately five years at the time of this recording.
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

This document is an informational/pr omotional walkthr ough of Purnima Mahayagya logistics — sankalp types (rakshasuraksha, jagriti, and standard negativity/pitru/kul devta sankalps), the akhand deepak program, and bhog/samagri of fering options.

Monetary figur es (parat costs, item categories) ar e recorded exactly as stated in the sour ce recording for documentary purposes and must never be presented by a bot as current, live pricing — see the Bot Response Guidelines in the accompanying Q&A document. Claimed effects (e.g., "50 to 500 dimensions," "20-25 days of shielding") ar e this teaching's own devotional metrics, not independently verifiable measur ements. The practitioner interview in Part D is personal testimony , not independently verified fact about the described physical recovery . This session has no separate Hinglish curated-conversation document — the interview segment is brief and lar gely procedural/promotional rather than substantive sangat dialogue.
